steps.title: One question, asked before every noun
steps.html:
English makes you answer a question before almost every noun: can my listener already tell which one I mean?

If they can — because it has been mentioned, because there is only one, because the sentence itself identifies it — use the. If they cannot, and you mean one of several, use a or an. If you are not talking about particular examples at all, but about a class of things, use no article with a plural or an uncountable noun.

steps.title: The cases that catch people out
steps.html:
• Describing versus identifying. She is the teacher points at one person we know. She is a teacher says what she does. Both are correct; they say different things.
  • General statements take no article. Festivals cost money. Not the festivals, unless you mean particular ones.
  • Uncountable nouns work the same way. Information is free in general; the information you sent is specific.
  • Names. No article with most countries, cities and people. But the with plural or descriptive names: the Netherlands, the United States, the Shetland Islands.
  • Superlatives and ordinals are definite by nature: the oldest, the first.

steps.title: Text A · A ceremony assembled in stages
steps.html:
Written for this course, from the Lerwick Up Helly Aa Committee’s own history of the festival.

On the last Tuesday in January, the town of Lerwick in Shetland burns a boat. The galley is a replica longship, built over about four months by people who will stand and watch it destroyed. At half past seven a rocket goes up, a thousand torches are lit, and the procession moves off through a crowd of five thousand or more. By ten in the evening there is nothing left of the winter’s work but ash.

The Norse history behind all this is perfectly real. The islands were settled from Norway more than a thousand years ago; a form of Norse was spoken here for centuries afterwards, and the settlers left their names on almost every hill. Plenty of families can find ancestors in the parish records, and the descendants of those families still work the same ground. What is a great deal younger than the costumes suggest is the festival itself.

Up Helly Aa grew out of tar barrelling, a rough midwinter custom in which squads of young men dragged barrels of burning tar through the streets on sledges, making trouble. Around 1870 a group of young men in the town replaced it with something better organised: a later date, elaborate disguise, and a torchlit parade. The Viking element arrived afterwards, in stages. A first sign of it appears in 1877; the galley itself only in the late 1880s; the title Guizer Jarl, worn by the chief guizer, not until 1906; and a Viking squad in the procession every single year only after the First World War. The ceremony people describe as ancient was established, piece by piece, by Victorians who admired a past they had never seen.

steps.title: Text B · Whose night is it?
steps.html:
Written for this course, from reporting by the BBC and Shetland.org.

None of that makes the festival false. A custom does not have to be old to be genuine; it has to be carried by a community that pays for it, builds it and turns up to it in the rain. Ancestry is not the qualification either. In practice a squad is formed among people who live in the town now — an immigrant of ten years’ standing can carry a torch, and a citizen by descent who moved to Aberdeen in 1998 cannot.

Living customs also argue with themselves. For roughly 142 years the Lerwick squads were open to men only; women organised the halls, the food and the all-night parties, and a good many of them defended that division firmly. Smaller fire festivals elsewhere in Shetland had female participants far earlier, and one of them appointed a woman as its Jarl in 2015. After a two-year gap caused by the pandemic, the Lerwick committee removed the restriction from the 2023 festival, and the following year the Jarl’s own squad included his daughter and three of his nieces. A tradition that can be amended is not a weaker tradition. It is a working one.

The other pressure comes from outside. The burning galley is the feature every camera wants, and the procession is now streamed live, which has made a town of seven thousand people known globally. The community has had to decide, more than once, how much of the night belongs to the visitors. So far the answer has been roughly this: the fire is yours to look at, and the twenty-four hours in the halls afterwards, which is where the festival actually lives, are ours.

steps.title: Напиши свой текст
steps.sub: Напиши ответ, затем сверься с образцом
steps.modelHtml:
Once a year, on the first Saturday in March, the village of Yelken holds a horse festival. The riders come down from the high pastures the night before, and by dawn there are three hundred horses in a field that is normally empty.

The festival is old, but not as old as visitors assume. The custom of racing in early spring goes back several centuries; the present form, with the ceremony at the well and the parade through the village, was established after the war, when the families who had returned wanted something to mark the first grass.

Photographs are welcome at the parade and at the races, which are the most photographed feature of the day. The ceremony at the well is not open, and we ask visitors to respect that. It lasts eleven minutes and it belongs to the families who lost people.

Come for the horses. Do not come expecting a show: the village is not performing, and there is nowhere to sit.
